topics.title: Introduction to Accounting Standards and GAAP
explain: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) are standard rules, procedures, and conventions that entities follow to prepare financial statements.
Accounting Standards (AS) are written policy documents issued by the Government and regulatory bodies to standardise accounting treatments.
Accounting Standards address four core aspects: Recognition, Measurement, Presentation, and Disclosure of financial transactions.
Key benefits of Accounting Standards include standardising accounting treatments, demanding additional useful disclosures, and ensuring comparability.
Comparability works at two levels: intra-enterprise (comparing the same company across different years) and inter-enterprise (comparing different companies in the same year).
Standardisation helps curb creative accounting, which is the practice of manipulating accounting policies to show favorable profits or assets.
If there is any conflict between a statutory law (statute) and an Accounting Standard, the law always prevails.

flow.title: Four Core Aspects Handled by Accounting Standards

topics.example: A company must explicitly disclose whether it calculates inventory cost using FIFO or Weighted Average method so investors can compare its performance accurately.
remember: Statute always prevails over Accounting Standards in case of any conflict.
mistakes: Confusing intra-enterprise comparison (comparing one firm over time) with inter-enterprise comparison (comparing two different firms).

quiz.q: What happens if there is a conflict between a statutory law and an Accounting Standard?
o: The matter is referred to IASB
quiz.why: Statute always overrides Accounting Standards in case of any legal conflict.

quiz.q: Comparing financial statements of the same enterprise across multiple financial years is known as:
quiz.why: Intra-enterprise comparison involves evaluating the performance of a single company over different time periods.

topics.title: Standards Setting Process in India
explain: The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) set up the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) in 1977 to formulate standards.
The ASB is an independent body comprising representatives from industry, regulators, government departments, and academia.
The standard-setting procedure follows an 8-step consultative process to ensure full transparency.

The steps start from identifying broad areas, forming study groups, preparing drafts, getting feedback from bodies, issuing Exposure Drafts, considering public comments, modifying drafts, and final issuance.
For non-corporate entities, Accounting Standards are issued directly by ICAI.
For corporate entities, NFRA recommends standards to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), which then notifies them.
Accounting Standard Interpretations (ASIs) were previously issued to clarify standards, but their consensus portions are now merged directly into the standards as 'Explanations'.
topics.example: When a new business model emerges, ASB forms a study group to draft a proposed standard, issues an Exposure Draft for public comment, and refines it before final issue.
remember: Out of 29 Accounting Standards issued by ICAI, effectively 27 exist today because AS 6 and AS 8 were withdrawn.
mistakes: Thinking MCA issues standards for non-corporate entities; non-corporate AS are issued by ICAI, while corporate AS are notified by MCA.

quiz.q: In which year was the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) constituted by ICAI?
quiz.why: ICAI constituted the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) in 1977.

quiz.q: How many effective Accounting Standards currently exist in India?
quiz.why: Out of 29 issued standards, AS 6 and AS 8 were withdrawn, leaving 27 active Accounting Standards.

topics.title: Global Accounting Standards and IASB
explain: Globalisation created a strong need for uniform financial reporting to help businesses raise international funds and enable cross-border comparisons.
The International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC) was formed in June 1973 in London by professional accounting bodies from over 75 countries.
In April 2001, the IASC was restructured into the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB).
Standards issued by IASC up to 31st March 2001 are called International Accounting Standards (IAS).
Standards issued by IASB from 1st April 2001 onwards are called International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).
The term IFRS includes IFRS issued by IASB, IAS issued by IASC, and interpretations issued by SIC and IFRIC.
IFRS are principles-based standards that establish broad rules rather than dictating rigid specific treatments.

flow.title: Components of International Financial Reporting Standards Framework

topics.example: An Indian firm listing shares on foreign stock exchanges uses IFRS-compliant financial reports so international investors can compare them easily with global peers.
remember: Standards issued before April 1, 2001 are IAS, while standards issued on or after April 1, 2001 are IFRS.
mistakes: Assuming IAS standards were abolished when IASB was formed; IASB adopted existing IAS standards, keeping them valid until revised.

quiz.q: When did the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) come into effect to replace IASC?
quiz.why: The restructured IASB came into effect on 1st April 2001.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT part of the overall IFRS framework?
quiz.why: Indian AS (Ind AS) are national standards issued by MCA, not part of the global IFRS framework issued by IASB/IASC.

topics.title: Adoption vs. Convergence and Carve Outs/Ins
explain: Countries can become IFRS compliant through either Direct Adoption or Convergence.
Adoption means applying IFRS exactly as issued by the IASB without any modification.
Convergence means developing local standards aligned with IFRS while making minor adjustments for national legal and economic environments.
India decided to converge with IFRS, resulting in Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS).
Carve-outs are deviations in Ind AS from IFRS principles to suit Indian economic conditions.
Carve-ins refer to additional guidance included in Ind AS over and above what is contained in IFRS.
Removing optional accounting treatments in Ind AS to maintain consistency does NOT count as a carve-out.
To number Ind AS corresponding to IFRS, add 100 to the IFRS number (e.g., IFRS 1 corresponds to Ind AS 101).

flow.title: Formulation Process of Ind AS from IFRS

topics.example: If Ind AS provides specific extra guidance for an accounting transaction not detailed in IFRS, that extra guidance is a Carve-in.
remember: To find the Ind AS number corresponding to an IFRS number, add 100 (e.g., IFRS 3 + 100 = Ind AS 103).
mistakes: Believing that removing accounting options creates a carve-out; standardizing options increases consistency without creating a carve-out.

quiz.q: Deviations in Ind AS from IFRS principles due to local economic conditions are called:
quiz.why: Carve-outs are deliberate deviations from IFRS principles made to suit Indian economic conditions.

quiz.q: What is the Ind AS number corresponding to IFRS 8 (Operating Segments)?
quiz.why: For standards corresponding to IFRS, add 100 to the IFRS number (8 + 100 = 108).

topics.title: Roadmap for Ind AS Implementation in India
explain: The MCA notified the roadmap for Ind AS implementation via notification dated 16th February 2015.
Companies (other than Banks, NBFCs, and Insurance firms) could apply Ind AS voluntarily from 1st April 2015.
Phase I (Mandatory from 1st April 2016): Listed or unlisted companies with Net Worth >= INR 500 crore, plus their parent, subsidiary, associate, and JV companies.
Phase II (Mandatory from 1st April 2017): All other listed companies (except SME exchange listed) and unlisted companies with Net Worth >= INR 250 crore but < INR 500 crore, plus group entities.
NBFCs followed a phased roadmap starting 1st April 2018 (Phase I: Net worth >= 500 crore) and 1st April 2019 (Phase II: Listed or unlisted Net worth >= 250 crore).
Implementation of Ind AS for Scheduled Commercial Banks and Insurance Companies has been deferred by RBI and IRDAI until further notice.
Companies listed exclusively on SME exchanges are exempt from Ind AS and continue using existing AS.
Once a company adopts Ind AS, it must continue following Ind AS for all future financial statements—there is no switching back.
topics.example: An unlisted company with a net worth of INR 350 crore must mandatorily implement Ind AS starting from Phase II (1st April 2017).
remember: Once Ind AS applies to an entity, there is no looking back; it must follow Ind AS for all subsequent years.
mistakes: Assuming SME exchange listed companies must adopt Ind AS; SME listed companies are specifically exempt and continue applying existing AS.

quiz.q: From which date was Ind AS implementation made mandatory for unlisted companies with a net worth of INR 600 crore?
quiz.why: Unlisted companies with net worth of INR 500 crore or more fell under Phase I mandatory implementation from 1st April 2016.

quiz.q: Which entities are exempted from mandatory Ind AS adoption and can continue using existing Accounting Standards?
o: Companies listed on main board stock exchange
Unlisted companies with net worth of INR 400 crore
NBFCs with net worth of INR 600 crore
quiz.why: Companies listed on SME exchanges are not required to apply Ind AS and continue applying existing AS.
